problems.reason: Polar form is described as r·e^{jθ}, and multiplying by adding angles relies on Euler's formula. For a learner who has only seen complex numbers briefly, polar form should need Euler's formula, not the other way round.
The unit-step description covers its relationship to the impulse (u[n] as a running sum of δ[n]). That needs δ[n], but only the continuous-time delta is linked, and it points the other way.
Energy and power are computed as integrals of |x(t)|^2 for continuous-time signals, but the concept only needs discrete-time signals.
The convolution theorem is stated for the continuous-time Fourier transform, and sampling uses it in continuous time, yet it only reaches discrete-time convolution through convolution-properties.
The rules 'causal iff h[n]=0 for n<0' and 'stable iff h is absolutely summable' come straight from the convolution sum, but the concept doesn't need convolution.
FIR filters are described as 'always stable', which follows from the absolute-summability test. There is no path from fir-filters to any stability concept.

Linear phase rests on the DTFT time-shift property (a delay becomes a linear phase factor). Nothing in the map needs dtft-properties, even though the learner wants the discrete-time side weighted more.

The z-transform ROC follows from geometric-series convergence, not the Laplace ROC. This arrow reflects syllabus order, not a real prerequisite, and it forces continuous-time material onto the discrete-time path the learner prefers.

Both cover linear constant-coefficient differential equations and their solutions. The syllabus assumes only Calculus II, so this material is taught in the course: merge the two into the taught concept.

The map has no inverse Laplace transform (partial fractions plus transform pairs), even though solving differential equations with the Laplace transform needs it. The z-domain side has inverse-z-transform.

The map lacks continuous-time stability and causality from poles and ROC (poles in the left half-plane, ROC includes the jω axis). Week 9 covers this, but stability-and-causality-from-poles only handles the z-plane.
Exams test whether a given system is memoryless as an apply-level problem, just like causality and linearity. Target depth should be 3, not 2.

concepts.name: Complex numbers
concepts.description: Numbers of the form a + jb, with their arithmetic, conjugates, magnitude, and representation as points in the complex plane.

concepts.name: Polar form of complex numbers
concepts.description: Writing a complex number as magnitude and angle, r·e^{jθ}, and multiplying or dividing complex numbers by combining their magnitudes and angles.

concepts.name: Euler's formula
concepts.description: The identity e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ, used to write sinusoids as sums of complex exponentials.

concepts.name: Trigonometric identities
concepts.description: Standard identities for sums, products, and phase shifts of sines and cosines.

concepts.name: Definite integrals
concepts.description: Computing the integral of a function over an interval, including piecewise functions and exponentials.

concepts.name: Improper integrals
concepts.description: Integrals over infinite intervals and the conditions under which they converge.

concepts.name: Integration by parts
concepts.description: An integration technique for products of functions, such as t·e^{-jωt}.

concepts.name: Summation notation
concepts.description: Reading and manipulating sigma-notation sums, including changing the index and splitting sums.

concepts.name: Geometric series
concepts.description: Closed-form sums of finite and infinite geometric series and the condition |r| < 1 for an infinite series to converge.

concepts.name: Linear ordinary differential equations
concepts.description: Linear constant-coefficient ODEs and their homogeneous and particular solutions.

concepts.name: Polynomial roots and factoring
concepts.description: Finding the roots of a polynomial, including complex-conjugate roots, and factoring it into linear terms.

concepts.name: Continuous-time signals
concepts.description: Signals x(t) defined for every real value of time t.

concepts.name: Discrete-time signals
concepts.description: Sequences x[n] defined only at integer indices n.

concepts.name: Signal energy and power
concepts.description: The total energy and average power of a signal, computed as an integral or sum of |x|^2.

concepts.name: Time shifting, scaling, and reversal
concepts.description: Transforming a signal's independent variable, as in x(at − b) or x[−n + k], and sketching the result.

concepts.name: Even and odd signal decomposition
concepts.description: Splitting any signal into an even part (x(t)+x(−t))/2 and an odd part (x(t)−x(−t))/2.

concepts.name: Periodic signals
concepts.description: Signals that repeat with a fundamental period, including the integer-period condition that applies to discrete-time sinusoids.

concepts.name: Complex exponential and sinusoidal signals
concepts.description: Signals of the form e^{st} or z^n, and in particular e^{jωn}, which describe sinusoids, growth, and decay.

concepts.name: Discrete-time unit impulse
concepts.description: The sequence δ[n], equal to 1 at n = 0 and 0 everywhere else, and its sifting property.

concepts.name: Unit step function
concepts.description: The step signals u(t) and u[n], their relationship to the impulse, and their use in writing signals that start at a given time.

concepts.name: Dirac delta function
concepts.description: The continuous-time impulse δ(t), defined by its sifting property under integration and equal to the derivative of the unit step.

concepts.name: Linearity
concepts.description: The property that a system obeys superposition (additivity and homogeneity), and how to test whether a given system has it.

concepts.name: Time invariance
concepts.description: The property that shifting a system's input in time shifts its output by the same amount, and how to test whether a given system has it.

concepts.name: Causality
concepts.description: The property that a system's output at any time depends only on present and past inputs.

concepts.name: BIBO stability
concepts.description: The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.

concepts.name: System memory
concepts.description: Whether a system's output depends only on the current input (memoryless) or also on other input values.

concepts.name: Linear time-invariant (LTI) systems
concepts.description: Systems that are both linear and time-invariant and are therefore fully described by their impulse response.

concepts.name: Impulse response
concepts.description: The output h of an LTI system when the input is a unit impulse.

concepts.name: Discrete-time convolution
concepts.description: Computing y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n−k] to find the output of a discrete-time LTI system.

concepts.name: Continuous-time convolution
concepts.description: Computing y(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t−τ) dτ, usually with the flip-and-slide method on piecewise signals.

concepts.name: Properties of convolution
concepts.description: Commutativity, associativity, and distributivity of convolution, and what they mean for systems connected in series and in parallel.

concepts.name: Causality and stability from the impulse response
concepts.description: An LTI system is causal if h is zero for negative time, and BIBO stable if h is absolutely summable or integrable.

concepts.name: Complex exponentials as eigenfunctions of LTI systems
concepts.description: A complex exponential passed through an LTI system comes out as the same exponential scaled by a complex gain.

concepts.name: Continuous-time Fourier series
concepts.description: Representing a periodic continuous-time signal as a sum of harmonically related complex exponentials, and computing the coefficients.

concepts.name: Discrete-time Fourier series
concepts.description: Representing a periodic sequence as a finite sum of N harmonically related discrete-time complex exponentials.

concepts.name: Continuous-time Fourier transform
concepts.description: The transform X(jω) = ∫ x(t)e^{-jωt} dt and its inverse, which describe aperiodic continuous-time signals in frequency.

concepts.name: Fourier transform properties
concepts.description: Linearity, time shift, frequency shift, scaling, duality, differentiation, and Parseval's relation for the Fourier transform.

concepts.name: Convolution theorem
concepts.description: Convolution in time corresponds to multiplication in frequency, and multiplication in time corresponds to convolution in frequency.

concepts.name: Sinc function
concepts.description: The function sin(πx)/(πx), which forms a Fourier transform pair with the rectangular pulse and is the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter.

concepts.name: Discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT)
concepts.description: The transform X(e^{jω}) = Σ x[n]e^{-jωn}, which is 2π-periodic in ω and describes sequences in frequency.

concepts.name: DTFT properties
concepts.description: Properties of the DTFT such as 2π periodicity, time shift as a linear phase factor, modulation, convolution, and symmetry for real signals.

concepts.name: Frequency response
concepts.description: H(e^{jω}), the Fourier transform of the impulse response, which gives the complex gain an LTI system applies at each frequency.

concepts.name: Magnitude and phase response
concepts.description: Splitting a frequency response into |H| and ∠H, plotting both (including on a dB scale), and reading off gain and delay.

concepts.name: Sampling
concepts.description: Turning a continuous-time signal into a sequence x[n] = x(nT), modeled as multiplication by an impulse train, which repeats the spectrum at multiples of the sampling frequency.

concepts.name: Nyquist sampling theorem
concepts.description: A bandlimited signal can be recovered exactly from its samples if the sampling rate is more than twice its highest frequency.

concepts.name: Aliasing
concepts.description: The overlap of repeated spectra when a signal is sampled too slowly, which makes high frequencies show up as lower frequencies.

concepts.name: Signal reconstruction
concepts.description: Recovering a continuous-time signal from its samples, either with ideal low-pass (sinc) interpolation or with practical hold circuits.

concepts.name: Normalized digital frequency
concepts.description: The relation ω = ΩT between continuous-time frequency in rad/s and discrete-time frequency in rad/sample, used to turn analog specifications into digital ones.

concepts.name: Laplace transform
concepts.description: The transform X(s) = ∫ x(t)e^{-st} dt, which extends the Fourier transform to complex frequencies s.

concepts.name: Region of convergence of the Laplace transform
concepts.description: The set of s values for which the Laplace integral converges, and how it depends on whether a signal is right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided.

concepts.name: Poles and zeros
concepts.description: The roots of the denominator and numerator of a rational transform, and how to plot them in the s-plane or z-plane.

concepts.name: Partial fraction expansion
concepts.description: Splitting a rational function into a sum of first-order terms so that each term can be inverse-transformed.

concepts.name: z-transform
concepts.description: The transform X(z) = Σ x[n]z^{-n}, which generalizes the DTFT and equals it on the unit circle.

concepts.name: Region of convergence of the z-transform
concepts.description: The annulus of z values where the z-transform sum converges, and what it implies about whether a sequence is right-sided, left-sided, or two-sided.

concepts.name: z-transform properties
concepts.description: Linearity, time shift as multiplication by z^{-k}, convolution as multiplication, and other z-transform properties.

concepts.name: Inverse z-transform
concepts.description: Recovering a sequence from X(z) and its ROC, using partial fractions, known transform pairs, or power-series expansion.

concepts.name: Stability and causality from poles and ROC
concepts.description: A causal discrete-time LTI system is stable when all its poles are inside the unit circle, which means its ROC includes the unit circle.

concepts.name: Linear constant-coefficient differential equations
concepts.description: Continuous-time LTI systems described by differential equations and solved with the Laplace transform.

concepts.name: Linear constant-coefficient difference equations
concepts.description: Recursive equations relating y[n] to past outputs and to current and past inputs, which describe discrete-time LTI filters.

concepts.name: Transfer function
concepts.description: The system function H(z) or H(s), equal to the ratio of the output and input transforms, which can be read directly from the difference or differential equation.

concepts.name: System block diagrams
concepts.description: Drawing a system as delays, gains, and adders, including direct-form realizations of a difference equation.

concepts.name: Frequency response from a pole-zero plot
concepts.description: Estimating the magnitude and phase response by looking at the vectors from the poles and zeros to points on the unit circle.

concepts.name: Ideal filters
concepts.description: Ideal low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass filters with brick-wall frequency responses, and why they cannot be built (their impulse responses are non-causal and infinitely long).

concepts.name: Filter specifications
concepts.description: Passband and stopband edges, transition width, passband ripple, and stopband attenuation as the requirements a practical filter must meet.

concepts.name: FIR filters
concepts.description: Filters with a finite-length impulse response, built without feedback, which are always stable.

concepts.name: IIR filters
concepts.description: Recursive filters with feedback and an infinite-length impulse response, whose poles must be placed so that the filter is stable.

concepts.name: Linear phase
concepts.description: A phase response that is linear in frequency, so all frequencies are delayed equally; symmetric FIR filters achieve it.

concepts.name: Moving-average filter
concepts.description: A simple FIR low-pass filter that averages the last M samples, and its frequency response.

concepts.name: Choosing FIR or IIR
concepts.description: Deciding between FIR and IIR filters by trading off linear phase, guaranteed stability, filter order, and computational cost.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.description: Rectangular, Hann, Hamming, and similar windows, and how each trades main-lobe width against sidelobe level.

concepts.name: Windowing method of FIR design
concepts.description: Designing an FIR filter by shifting and truncating an ideal impulse response, then multiplying it by a window.

concepts.name: Filter design by pole-zero placement
concepts.description: Designing a simple IIR filter, such as a first-order low-pass, by placing poles and zeros to shape the magnitude response.

concepts.name: Digital low-pass filter design
concepts.description: Turning a low-pass specification into a working digital filter, then checking its frequency response, stability, and implementation.
